title: Cygnus X-1 binary star system
caption: The Cygnus X-1 black hole system and its jet bowshock, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and H. Schweiker (WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Near the center of this wide view sit two stars, and the brighter, lower one is Cygnus X-1. It looks like a single star, but it is actually a binary system that contains a black hole. Above it, at top center, curves a bluish shape like an umbrella, and bright orange gas spreads along the left side.

In Cygnus X-1, the black hole pulls gas away from its companion star. Before the gas falls in, it grows so hot that it gives off X-rays, which is how the system was discovered. Not all of it is swallowed, and some is launched outwards in jets of hot gas.

The jet itself is invisible, but its effect shows. The bluish umbrella is a bowshock, formed where gas in the jet slams into gas in the surrounding nebula. The orange glow on the left belongs to Sharpless 101, an emission nebula whose western edge reaches into the frame.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope recorded light from specific glowing gases. According to the caption, hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and sulfur [S II] in blue, though the source's filter table lists oxygen [O III] and hydrogen-alpha filters.
filters: 499 nm · Optical Olll (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
656 nm · Optical Ha (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate light from individual gases, so faint structures like the bowshock stand out in a way the eye could never see.

explore: Kitt Peak National Observatory's Mayall 4-meter telescope took the image using its wide-field Mosaic camera. North is up and east is to the left.
alt: A star field with a bluish umbrella-shaped arc at top center, two stars near the middle, and orange glowing gas along the left side.
